state.target_passage: Thanks for kicking this off; I'll take the first concrete design decision on site placement and the accompanying data schema so we have something to iterate on. For our neighborhood site I'm proposing we anchor all primary sensors—temperature, relative humidity, barometric pressure, and a two-component rain gauge—on a single 1.5 m mast positioned at least 10 m from any building roofline, tree canopy edge, or paved surface, ideally over bare mowed grass on a south-facing slope with unobstructed view of the sky in all azimuths, and we treat that mast as our only "reference point" so every reading in the log is traceable to one defined coordinate (latitude/longitude to six decimals, local time zone, UTC offset, and a fixed grid reference we photograph into the record). The record-keeping schema I'm locking in now is a minimal relational structure: an observation table (timestamp in UTC, instrument ID, sensor type, raw value, units, quality flag 0-4, observer initials), an instrument table (make/model/serial, installation date, last calibration date, calibration method, known offset, next-due calibration date), and a site-conditions table (weather at time of reading, wind speed/direction, any anomaly noted, photo reference number), with every row hash-chained daily into a local JSON file that gets mirrored to a shared drive—no one edits a past row, only appends a correction row that cites the original. On the failure side, the concrete danger I want us to engineer around is thermal-inertia bias from a poorly shielded sensor: in a real case a volunteer station in Tucson, Arizona, mounted its temperature sensor on the north wall of a cinder-block garage and never noticed that the July afternoon readings ran 4–5 °C below the co-located NWS Mesonet mast because the concrete radiated stored heat asymmetrically and the sensor's ventilation was partially blocked by a water meter bracket; the bias was smooth and seasonally correlated, so a simple "mean offset" QC pass missed it entirely, and three months of monthly-mean summaries were quietly contaminated before anyone cross-checked against the neighbor station. To prevent exactly that, our protocol mandates a same-day, same-elevation cross-check against at least one nearby public station within 15 km, and any persistent offset exceeding 0.5 °C or 3 hPa triggers a forced recalibration and a site-survey walk before the next observation cycle, logged in the site-conditions table with photos of the mast's immediate surroundings so the record itself becomes the defense against slow, invisible drift.
